title: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

matcher.pattern: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

jokes: Docker Desktop isn't running. It never is, when you need it.
The Docker daemon is asleep and you didn't wake it up.
You ran a docker command with no daemon listening. Classic.
Docker is not running. Have you tried turning it on?
This is the docker equivalent of yelling into an empty room.

fix.summary: Start Docker Desktop or the docker daemon service.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Docker Desktop isn't running. It never is. Start it and try again like the rest of us.
The daemon's down. Open Docker Desktop, wait the obligatory thirty seconds, retry.

title: port is already allocated

matcher.pattern: Bind for [\d.]+:(\d+) failed: port is already allocated

jokes: Port {port} is already claimed by another container. Or the last one you forgot to stop.
You have a zombie container squatting on port {port}.
Port {port} is taken, probably by yesterday's forgotten `docker run`.
This container wants port {port}, but so does something you already started.
You have too many containers and not enough ports.

fix.summary: Stop the container using that port, or map to a different one.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Port {port} is already bound. Probably to the container you forgot to stop last time.
Something's already on {port}. docker ps will tell you what. Check before you complain.

title: pull access denied / image not found
jokes: '{image}' doesn't exist, or it's private and you're not invited.
Docker Hub has no idea what '{image}' is.
You're pulling '{image}' and getting nothing but rejection.
That image name is either misspelled or belongs to someone else's registry.
'{image}': pull denied, dreams denied.

fix.summary: Check the image name/tag, and log in if it's a private registry.

title: no space left on device
jokes: Docker has quietly eaten your entire disk with old layers.
No space left on device: every image you never pruned is now haunting you.
Your disk is full of dangling images from six months ago.
This is what happens when you never run docker system prune.
Docker's cache grew into a monster and it just ate your free space.

fix.summary: Prune unused Docker images, containers, and volumes.

sarcastic-senior-dev: No disk space left. Docker's been hoarding old images and layers for months. Run a prune.
You're out of space. This happens to everyone who's never run docker system prune.

title: container exited with non-zero code
jokes: Your container exited with code {code}. It had thoughts and they were bad.
Exit code {code}: the container's way of saying something went wrong inside.
That container ran, then immediately regretted it. Exit {code}.
Container exit code {code}. Time to check the logs.
The entrypoint failed and left exit code {code} as evidence.

fix.summary: Check the container logs for the real error.

title: npm ERR! ERESOLVE
jokes: npm found conflicting dependency requirements and gave up trying to guess.
ERESOLVE: your dependency tree is arguing with itself.
Two packages want different versions of the same thing. npm refuses to referee.
This is the price of a deep and tangled node_modules tree.
npm's dependency resolver just threw its hands up.

fix.summary: Resolve manually, or retry with --legacy-peer-deps if appropriate.

title: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'package.json'
jokes: There's no package.json here. You're not in a Node project, or not in the right folder.
npm looked for package.json and found empty air.
This directory has no package.json. It never claimed to be a Node project.
You ran npm somewhere that isn't a Node project. Bold move.
package.json is missing. So is the plan.

fix.summary: cd into the project root, or run npm init if starting fresh.

title: EACCES permission denied
jokes: npm wants root, or at least ownership of its own directories.
EACCES: npm's global install directory doesn't trust you.
You tried a global install without the right permissions. Classic npm rite of passage.
Permission denied. npm's global folder has trust issues, usually because you once used sudo.
This is the direct result of installing Node with sudo at some point in your life.

fix.summary: Fix npm's global directory ownership rather than using sudo.

title: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement

matcher.pattern: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement ([\w.\-\[\]]+)

jokes: '{package}' doesn't exist on PyPI, at least not with that name or version.
pip searched everywhere for '{package}' and found nothing that fits.
'{package}': not on PyPI, not in your Python version's compatibility range, not happening.
You asked pip for a version of '{package}' that simply isn't published.
This is either a typo or a version that was never released.

fix.summary: Check the package name/version and your Python version compatibility.

title: externally-managed-environment
jokes: Your system Python is protected from itself, and now from you too.
pip refuses to install globally into a system-managed Python. This is a feature.
Modern Python is tired of you breaking your OS packages. Use a venv.
This is PEP 668 telling you, politely but firmly, to use a virtual environment.
System Python said no. It's not personal, it's PEP 668.

fix.summary: Use a virtual environment instead of installing into system Python.

title: docker-compose version unsupported
jokes: Your compose file claims a version that this Compose install has never heard of.
docker-compose and your compose.yml disagree on what year it is.
That version key is either too old or too new for the Compose binary you have.
This is a compatibility mismatch between the compose spec and your installed tooling.
Someone wrote this file for a different Compose than the one running it.
The compose file version and the compose CLI version are not on speaking terms.

fix.summary: Update the compose file's version key, or install a Compose version that supports it.

title: volume mount permission denied

matcher.pattern: Error response from daemon: .*: permission denied

jokes: The container can see the mounted volume, but it isn't allowed to touch it.
Permission denied inside the container, because the host and container users disagree on ownership.
This is the classic UID mismatch between your host user and the container's user.
Docker mounted the volume just fine. The permissions came along for the ride, unfortunately.
Your bind mount works. Reading or writing to it does not.
Somewhere, a chmod or a matching UID would have prevented this entirely.

fix.summary: Match the container user's UID/GID to the host, or adjust the mounted directory's permissions.

title: network not found

matcher.pattern: Error response from daemon: network ([\w-]+) not found

jokes: The network '{network}' doesn't exist. Someone removed it, or it was never created.
You're trying to attach to '{network}', which is not a real network right now.
'{network}' was probably torn down by a docker-compose down at some point.
This container wants to join '{network}' and '{network}' isn't home.
Docker networks don't persist by magic. '{network}' needs to be created first.
'{network}' not found: check for a typo or a missing docker network create.

fix.summary: Create the network, or bring up the compose stack that defines it.

title: npm ERR! 404 Not Found
jokes: npm asked the registry for '{url}' and got a 404 for its trouble.
That package doesn't exist on the registry, or its name is misspelled.
'{url}': the registry has never heard of this package.
This is either a typo, an unpublished package, or a private package you're not logged into.
npm went looking at '{url}' and found nothing but a 404.
The registry says no such package exists. It's usually right.

fix.summary: Check the package name for typos, or log in if it's a private package.

title: npm ERR! missing script
jokes: There is no '{script}' script in package.json. You made that name up just now.
npm run '{script}' assumes '{script}' exists. It does not.
Check package.json's scripts block, because '{script}' is not in it.
'{script}' is not a real npm script, no matter how confidently you typed it.
This project has scripts. '{script}' is simply not one of them.
You ran a script that was never defined. npm is just the messenger.

fix.summary: Check the scripts block in package.json for the correct script name.

title: npm ERR! unsupported engine
jokes: This package wants a Node version you don't currently have.
EBADENGINE: your Node version and this package's requirements don't match.
Somewhere in package.json, an engines field is judging your Node install.
This is what happens when the project was built against a newer, or older, Node.
Your Node version is technically wrong for this package, according to the package itself.
The engines field exists specifically to produce this error.

fix.summary: Switch to the Node version this package expects, e.g. with nvm.

title: npm ci: package.json and lockfile out of sync

matcher.pattern: npm ERR! `npm ci` can only install packages when your package\.json and package-lock\.json

jokes: package.json changed and nobody regenerated the lockfile. npm ci noticed immediately.
This is npm ci doing exactly what it's designed to do: refuse to guess.
Your lockfile and package.json disagree, and CI mode does not tolerate disagreement.
Someone edited a dependency by hand without running npm install afterward.
npm ci is strict on purpose. Your lockfile just failed that strictness test.
This is the reason lockfiles exist, and also the reason they get out of sync.

fix.summary: Run npm install to regenerate the lockfile, then commit it.

title: is not a supported wheel on this platform

matcher.pattern: is not a supported wheel on this platform

jokes: That wheel was built for a different OS, architecture, or Python version than yours.
This binary package simply was not made for the machine you're running.
The wheel exists. It just doesn't exist for your platform.
Someone built this for a different CPU architecture, and it shows.
pip found the package but not a build that matches your setup.
This is what cross-platform wheel mismatches look like in practice.

fix.summary: Check for a wheel matching your Python version/platform, or install from source.

title: SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED
jokes: pip doesn't trust the certificate chain between you and PyPI right now.
This is a corporate proxy, an expired cert, or a misconfigured trust store. Pick one.
SSL verification failed, which is usually a sign something is intercepting your traffic.
pip refuses to talk to a server it can't verify. That's the correct instinct.
Somewhere between you and the package index, a certificate stopped checking out.
This is your OS's trust store having a disagreement with PyPI's certificate.

fix.summary: Fix your system's certificate trust store, or configure the correct proxy/CA bundle.

title: Could not open requirements file

matcher.pattern: ERROR: Could not open requirements file.*No such file or directory: '([^']+)'

jokes: '{path}' doesn't exist. Neither does the install you were hoping for.
pip looked for '{path}' and found nothing but a wrong working directory.
You're not in the folder you think you're in, and '{path}' proves it.
'{path}' is a path to nowhere, as far as pip is concerned.
This is usually a wrong directory, not a missing file.
requirements.txt exists somewhere. Just not at '{path}'.

fix.summary: Check you're in the right directory and the requirements file name is correct.

title: ImportError: cannot import name 'main' from 'pip'
jokes: Something is calling pip's old internal API, which stopped existing several major versions ago.
pip.main() was removed years ago and this script never got the memo.
This is a script written for an ancient pip, running against a modern one.
pip's internals are not a public API, and this is exactly why that rule exists.
You upgraded pip and broke a script that was quietly relying on its guts.
This has been broken since pip stopped exposing main() directly. That was a while ago.

fix.summary: Update the script to call pip via subprocess (python -m pip) instead of importing its internals.

title: No matching distribution found

matcher.pattern: ERROR: No matching distribution found for ([\w.\-\[\]]+)

jokes: '{package}' has no distribution that fits your Python version or platform.
pip searched every index it knows and '{package}' just isn't there for you.
This is either a typo, a private package with no index configured, or a genuine gap.
'{package}' exists somewhere, probably. Not somewhere pip can currently reach.
No matching distribution: the more mysterious cousin of package-not-found.
Check your index URL, because '{package}' might just be on a different one.

fix.summary: Check the package name, your Python version, and any custom index URLs.
